newsitem.title: USA: Government opens case against Staples merger.
newsitem.headline: Government opens case against Staples merger.

text.p: The government opened its case Monday against the planned $4 billion merger of Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. arguing the combined company would raise prices on everything from file folders to copy paper.
With the chief executives of both companies sitting at the defense table, their lead attorney opened his case by declaring there was "no doubt" the merged company would offer consumers lower prices.

The five-day hearing before Judge Thomas Hogan will give both sides a chance to call witnesses and present evidence before the judge rules whether to grant the Federal Trade Commission a preliminary injunction against the merger.
If he does, a long trial before an FTC law judge would follow.
But Staples CEO Thomas Stemberg said that, win or lose, he plans to take the case no further. He told Reuters that so far Staples and Office Depot have spent $12 million in legal fees.
The five-member Federal Trade Commission has already voted twice to halt the merger, but must prove its case in court.
George Cary, chief lawyer for the FTC, presented a series of internal documents in which Office Depot and Staples identified each other as their major competitors for office supplies.

"In 20 years of practicing antitrust law, we have something here I have never seen before -- real evidence, rich evidence from the companies' own documents," Cary told the judge. "This requires no guesswork."
Office superstores first appeared in the mid-1980s and dramatically lowered prices for office supplies. But Cary argued that the situation had changed at Staples.

A July 19, 1996, memo to Staples CEO Stemberg said that Staples had "dramatic rate increases over the last five years in part due to our policy on all non-PSI (price sensitive items) and invisible items."

FTC lawyer Cary said that meant they could raise profits and prices on "invisible" and "non-price sensitive" items, where customers fail to notice price increases. But Cary said the fly in the ointment was competition from Office Depot.
The internal Staples memo said, "Office Depot (has) worked on much lower margins and today their aggressive market prices indicates that is probably still true."
Because of competition, Staples would have to achieve "pricing parity" with Office Depot, an internal memo said. Cary said that translates into lower prices.
The government offered evidence based on internal company documents showing prices were lowest on average where Office Depot, Staples and another chain, OfficeMax Inc., competed.

But prices were as much as 14 percent higher where Staples or Office Depot faced no competition from another office superstore. The differences persisted even if the office superstores were near a K-Mart, WalMart, or another large store that also sold some office supplies.
But the lead attorney for the two chains, Don Kempf, said consumers were happy to see even one office superstore opening in an area where there are none.

"They celebrate us coming to town," he said. "They aren't bemoaning the fact that prices are lower in Los Angeles, they're celebrating because prices are 37 percent to 50 percent lower" than other stores.
Kempf gave his own examples of price comparisons, showing that in some cases prices are lower where there are only two office superstores competing instead of three.
And he ridiculed the averages cited by the FTC.
"It's a classic example of confusion between correlation and causation," he said. "It's like saying hospitals must be dangerous because so many people die there. This is utter nonsense."
He said the merger was "no threat to the prices of consumable office supplies."
Kempf also demonstrated the competition he said exists by playing a Staples television commercial, a radio commercial and other media offerings.
